newsitem.title: USA: NJ Supreme Court orders $248 mln for poor schools.
newsitem.headline: NJ Supreme Court orders $248 mln for poor schools.

text.p: The New Jersey Supreme Court Wednesday rejected the school aid formula in Gov. Christie Whitman's public education reforms and ordered the administration to budget $248 million more for the 28 districts identified earlier as having special needs.
That ruling was a sweeping victory for the poor districts, and a repudiation of almost every argument the administration made in a March 4 hearing.
Whitman said the ruling disappointed her but she would be able to comply, in large part because she was getting a lot more revenues than expected this year from tax collections.

Treasurer Brian Clymer estimated the state will have collected $450 million more than budgeted by June 30, the end of the fiscal year. The non-partisan Office of Legislative Services was even more optimistic, putting the bonus at $700 million.
Whitman said state aid would not be diverted from high- and middle-income districts to comply with the order.
"I applaud the Supreme Court for putting the children first," said Superintendent Roy Dawson of the Camden schools, which will benefit from the court's decision.
The outlook in Paulsboro was somewhat different.

The relatively poor, small Gloucester County town met all the tests for being included as a special needs district, said Superintendent of Schools Walter C. Quint. He said those needs were finally recognized in Whitman's new plan.
"I'm concerned that our deal might unravel if we have to start from scratch" because of the new ruling, Quint said.

The high court voted to affirm a deadline it set in 1994, but for the first time there was a dissent. Justice Marie L. Garibaldi said she would have given the administration another year to show its plan could work.

The administration had hoped to alter the terms of the debate by setting curriculum standards. These would define constitutional levels of learning and relieve it of the need to match the spending power of the state's wealthiest districts.
In 1990, the court had ruled that the state was responsible for seeing to it that the poorest 28 districts had the per pupil spending power to match the average of the top 120.
"Does this mean we will always be chasing the highest spending districts? Or do we have to impose caps?" Whitman asked.
